title: The Baba Sali
hookLine: Rabbi Israel Abuhatzeira, a Moroccan sage loved for his blessings and humility
tomorrow: so many voices, across so many years. how do they fit on one page?

cards: Before a big exam, a grandmother puts her hand on your head and says something under her breath, and walks back to the stove like it was nothing. It wasn't nothing.
Somewhere in Morocco, and later in a small town in Israel, people lined up to see one old rabbi. They weren't there for a lecture or a ruling.
They came with a sick child, a business about to fail, a marriage, a move, and they asked for a blessing.

teach.b: His name was Rabbi Israel Abuhatzeira, and people called him the Baba Sali, a Moroccan Arabic name often rendered as the praying father.

Tradition remembers him for two things that went together: blessings, and humility. Here's why they go together, from the Torah itself. The priestly blessing in Numbers begins: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee."
The priests say the words. But then God says, "I will bless them." The one speaking is a messenger, not the source.
So the people best at blessing are often the ones who know they aren't the point.
A blessing from someone humble passes straight through. It also means a blessing never needed a grand person.
On Friday nights, Jewish parents rest their hands on their children's heads and say these same words from Numbers: a tired mother after a long week, a grandfather in his slippers.
The words aren't theirs either, and that is exactly what lets them carry. And asking for one takes a little humility too: you admit you can't hand yourself everything you need.
That's today's line, and it ties the week together: every voice since Fackenheim was handing on something bigger than themselves.

how: Jewish parents bless their children on Friday night, hands on their heads, often with the priestly blessing from Numbers 6; Moroccan Jewish families visit the graves of sages like the Baba Sali to ask for blessings.

games.q: your aunt is well-known in the family for her blessings at every simcha. someone praises her to her face. by today's lesson, what's the likely reply?
o: it isn't mine; i just say the words.
thank you, i've worked hard to get good at it.
you're right, my blessings work better than most.
games.why: in Numbers the priests speak and God says, I will bless them. the humble know they're a messenger, which is why a blessing passes straight through them.

practice: Think of one older person whose good wishes you'd want: a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor. Write them a short message asking, plainly, for their blessing, or just their good wishes, before something coming up.
Send it now if you're ready, or keep it ready to send. Then read your own words once, and notice what it took to ask.
